title: Design principles
scopeHtml: Scope: DRY, KISS, YAGNI, Law of Demeter, tell-don't-ask, composition over inheritance, separation of concerns, fail fast, least astonishment, immutability, and how they conflict.

notes.title: Why principles, not rules
notes.html:
Design principles are rules of thumb that predict which code will be cheap to change. They conflict sometimes (DRY pushes you to merge, YAGNI pushes you not to abstract yet), so a senior's skill is knowing which wins here and why. The cost being fought is always the same: the price of the next change.

Worked example. A feature touches 1 file in a well-designed module (1 hour) versus 9 files in a tangled one (1.5 days). Over 40 features a year that is 40 hours against 480 hours, a team-month, caused by design not typing speed.

Industry examples. Google's engineering practices doc favours readable, simple code over clever code. Basecamp and early Instagram stayed small on purpose (YAGNI at company scale).

Everyday analogy. Kitchen habits: label things (DRY), simple recipes (KISS), buy only what you will cook (YAGNI).

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting acronyms with no example of when a principle should be broken.
  • Treating principles as laws rather than trade-offs.

notes.title: DRY: one source of truth
notes.html:
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) means each piece of knowledge lives in exactly one place. It is about knowledge, not about identical-looking lines.

Before (the same rule in 3 places):

// OrderService
if (user.getAge() >= 18 && user.isVerified()) { ... }
// SignupController
if (age >= 18 && verified) { ... }
// ReportJob: someone changed it to > 18 (bug)
if (u.getAge() > 18 && u.isVerified()) { ... }

After:

final class Eligibility {
    static final int ADULT_AGE = 18;
    static boolean canPurchase(User u) { return u.age() >= ADULT_AGE && u.verified(); }
}
object Eligibility { const val ADULT_AGE = 18; fun canPurchase(u: User) = u.age >= ADULT_AGE && u.verified }

Worked example. The rule changes from 18 to 21 for a market: 1 edit versus finding 3 (and missing the one using >). A real incident pattern is two services computing "active subscription" differently, so billing charges users that the app shows as cancelled; the metric is a mismatch between billing count and active-user count.

Industry examples. OpenAPI schemas or protobuf files generate client and server code from one definition (single source of truth). Shopify and Stripe generate SDKs from API specs.

Everyday analogy. One master calendar everyone reads, instead of everyone keeping their own copy that drifts.

Decision gravity. Merging duplicates is reversible when they are internal. Sharing code between services via a common library couples their release cycles; that is close to a one-way door. Also, two things that look identical but change for different reasons are not duplicates: merging them (accidental duplication) creates a worse coupling than the copy. Wait for the rule of three.

Common interview traps.

  • Over-DRYing: a function with 8 boolean flags to serve 2 "similar" callers.
  • Forgetting DRY applies to config, schemas, docs and tests, not just code.

notes.title: KISS: keep it simple
notes.html:
KISS says choose the simplest design that meets the requirement. Simple means few moving parts and easy to explain, not "fewest lines".

Before (clever):

// 1 line, nobody can debug it
return Optional.ofNullable(u).map(User::cart).map(c -> c.items().stream()
    .filter(i -> i.qty() > 0).mapToLong(i -> i.price() * i.qty()).sum()).orElse(0L);

After (plain):

long total = 0;
if (u == null || u.cart() == null) return 0;
for (Item i : u.cart().items()) total += i.price() * i.qty();
return total;
fun total(u: User?): Long = u?.cart?.items?.sumOf { it.price * it.qty } ?: 0L

The Kotlin version is both short and clear; simplicity depends on the idiom of the language.

Worked example. A team added a message broker, 3 microservices and a saga for a feature serving 200 requests/day. A monolith with one transaction would handle 100x that on a single db.t3.medium. Operational cost: 3 deploy pipelines, on-call load, tracing. Simple would have shipped in 2 weeks instead of 3 months.

Industry examples. Stack Overflow served huge traffic with a small number of well-tuned servers. Basecamp ("majestic monolith"). Amazon Prime Video moved a monitoring service from distributed Lambda/Step Functions back to a single process and reported large cost savings (confirm figures in their engineering blog).

Everyday analogy. A hammer for a nail, not a robotic nailing arm.

Decision gravity. Choosing simple first is reversible: you can add complexity when a measured need appears. Premature complexity (distributed system, plug-in framework) is the expensive one-way door because you pay its cost every day.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing "simple" with "easy": a framework you already know is easy, but may not be simple.
  • Presenting a 12-box architecture for a CRUD app.

notes.title: YAGNI: you aren't gonna need it
notes.html:
YAGNI says do not build something because you might need it later. Speculative features cost time now, code to maintain, and are usually guessed wrong.

Before (speculative generality):

interface ExportStrategy { }
abstract class AbstractExporterFactoryProvider { }
class ExporterRegistry { /* plugin loader for formats, "in case we add PDF, XML, Parquet" */ }
// real requirement today: export CSV

After:

void exportCsv(List<Order> orders, Writer out) throws IOException {
    for (Order o : orders) out.write(o.id() + "," + o.total() + "\n");
}
fun exportCsv(orders: List<Order>, out: Appendable) = orders.forEach { out.append("${it.id},${it.total}\n") }

When the second format actually arrives, extract an interface then (a 20-minute refactor with tests).

Worked example. The plug-in framework: 3 days to build, 600 lines, 2 bugs, and 3 formats never added. Cost over two years including reading and maintaining: roughly 10 engineer-days for zero use. Industry studies (and the "Standish"-style numbers often quoted) suggest a large share of features are rarely used; treat such figures as folklore unless you can cite them, and measure your own usage with analytics.

Industry examples. Extreme Programming (Kent Beck, Ron Jeffries) coined it. Many startups ship a single-region, single-DB v1 and add sharding only at about 70% of measured capacity.

Everyday analogy. Not buying a canoe because you might move to a lake house.

Decision gravity. YAGNI is safe when the change is cheap later (adding a class, a column, an endpoint). It is wrong when the change is a one-way door that is cheap now and ruinous later: for example, adding an id and a created_at to every table, UTC timestamps, API versioning, idempotency keys on payments. Those are not speculation, they are known costs of retrofit.

Common interview traps.

  • Using YAGNI as an excuse to skip tests, security or migrations.
  • Not distinguishing "the requirement exists, just later" (plan for it) from "someone might want it" (do not build).

notes.title: Law of Demeter: talk to friends
notes.html:
The Law of Demeter (least knowledge) says an object should only call methods on itself, its fields, its parameters, and objects it created. Avoid a.getB().getC().doThing() train wrecks.

Before:

String city = order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity();     // knows 3 classes
double fee = order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCountry().getTaxRule().rate();

After:

class Order {
    String shippingCity() { return customer.shippingCity(); }
}
class Customer {
    String shippingCity() { return address.city(); }
}
String city = order.shippingCity();
class Order(private val customer: Customer) { fun shippingCity() = customer.shippingCity() }

Worked example. If Address.city is renamed to a Location object, the "before" version breaks in every one of 40 callers; the "after" version changes only Customer.shippingCity(). Count the dots in a line (more than 2 across different types) as a smell, but a fluent builder or stream chain on one type (list.stream().filter().map()) is fine.

Industry examples. Hibernate lazy-loading plus deep chains in views produces N+1 queries and LazyInitializationException. Android's context.getResources().getDisplayMetrics().density is a Demeter violation that tests struggle to fake.

Everyday analogy. You ask your friend to pass the salt; you do not reach into their pocket for their wallet.

Decision gravity. Adding delegating methods is cheap but can bloat classes with pass-through methods (middle man). It is a trade: fewer callers coupled to internals versus more surface. Reversible.

Common interview traps.

  • Counting dots mechanically; the real rule is about knowledge of structure, and data transfer objects with plain getters are exempt.
  • Fixing with dozens of one-line wrappers instead of moving the behaviour (see tell, don't ask).

notes.title: Tell, don't ask
notes.html:
Tell, don't ask means tell an object what to do instead of pulling its data out and deciding for it. Behaviour belongs next to the data it uses.

Before (ask, then decide outside):

if (account.getBalance() >= amount && account.getStatus() == Status.ACTIVE) {
    account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - amount);
} else {
    throw new IllegalStateException();
}

After (tell):

account.withdraw(amount);          // the account checks its own rules
account.withdraw(amount)
 Before: Caller reads balance, status, then writes balance   (logic duplicated in every caller)
 After:  Caller --withdraw()--> Account { rules + state }    (logic once)

Worked example. Check-then-act outside the object has a race: two threads read balance 1000, both withdraw 700. Moving the logic inside lets the object (or its database UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= 700) make it atomic. It also removes the same check copied across 12 callers, one of which forgot the status test.

Industry examples. Anemic domain models (Fowler's anti-pattern) in Spring apps put all logic in *Service classes with entities as data bags; rich domain models in DDD put behaviour on the entity. Actor systems (Akka, Erlang) enforce tell by design: you send messages, you cannot read internal state.

Everyday analogy. Tell the waiter "I'd like the pasta"; do not walk into the kitchen to check stock and cook it yourself.

Decision gravity. Moving logic into entities is reversible. Not every read is a violation: queries, reports and DTOs legitimately ask (CQRS separates the read side). Use judgement.

Common interview traps.

  • Dogmatic: "never use getters". Views and serialisation need them.
  • Treating it as the same as Demeter; they overlap but Demeter is about reach, this is about where logic lives.

notes.title: Composition over inheritance
notes.html:
Prefer building behaviour by combining small objects over extending a parent class. Has-a with delegation is more flexible than is-a.

Before (inheritance explosion):

class Bird { void fly() { } }
class Penguin extends Bird { void fly() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); } }  // LSP violation
// add swimming, loud, trained... : FlyingSwimmingBird, FlyingLoudBird ...

After (compose abilities):

interface Movement { void move(); }
class Flying implements Movement { public void move() { /* flap */ } }
class Swimming implements Movement { public void move() { /* paddle */ } }

class Animal {
    private Movement movement;                       // swappable at runtime
    Animal(Movement m) { this.movement = m; }
    void setMovement(Movement m) { this.movement = m; }
    void go() { movement.move(); }
}
Animal penguin = new Animal(new Swimming());
interface Movement { fun move() }
class Animal(private var movement: Movement) { fun go() = movement.move() }
// Kotlin delegation removes the forwarding boilerplate:
class Duck(m: Movement) : Movement by m
 Inheritance: Bird <- FlyingBird <- LoudFlyingBird ...  (combinatorial)
 Composition: Animal --has--> Movement (Flying | Swimming) , Sound (Loud | Quiet)

Worked example. 3 movement types x 3 sound types = 9 subclasses by inheritance versus 3 + 3 = 6 small classes with composition, and no new class when you add a 4th sound (only 1). Changing behaviour at runtime (a bird swapping to Swimming) is impossible with inheritance, trivial with composition.

Industry examples. Android moved from deep Activity inheritance to ViewModel, LifecycleObserver and Jetpack Compose (functions composed together). The Strategy, Decorator and Composite patterns in the GoF book are all composition; the book itself states the principle. Go and Rust have no class inheritance at all.

Everyday analogy. Lego bricks you snap together versus a one-piece moulded toy.

Decision gravity. Starting with composition is cheap and reversible; starting with inheritance is a one-way door, since removing a base class means rewriting subclasses and every caller relying on the supertype. Inheritance remains right for a stable, true is-a with real code reuse (for example AbstractList).

Common interview traps.

  • "Never use inheritance": false, but justify each use.
  • Delegation boilerplate: Kotlin by, Lombok @Delegate, or IDE generation helps.
  • Fragile base class: a child that depends on how the parent calls its own methods.

notes.title: Separation of concerns and fail fast
notes.html:
Separation of concerns (SoC) means each part of the code deals with one concern. Layers are the typical example: controller handles HTTP, service handles business rules, repository handles storage. Fail fast means detect a problem at the earliest point and stop loudly, instead of passing bad data along.

Before (mixed concerns, late failure):

@PostMapping("/pay")
String pay(@RequestBody Map<String,Object> body) {
    String amt = (String) body.get("amount");                          // could be null
    Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(URL);                   // SQL inside controller
    c.createStatement().execute("UPDATE wallet SET bal = bal - " + amt);  // SQL injection, NPE later
    return "ok";
}

After:

record PayRequest(@NotNull @Positive Long cents, @NotBlank String walletId) { }

@PostMapping("/pay")
void pay(@Valid @RequestBody PayRequest r) { walletService.debit(r.walletId(), r.cents()); }   // HTTP concern

class WalletService {                                                                          // business concern
    void debit(String id, long cents) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(id);
        if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("cents");
        repo.debit(id, cents);
    }
}
data class PayRequest(val cents: Long, val walletId: String) {
    init { require(cents > 0) { "cents must be positive" }; require(walletId.isNotBlank()) }
}

Worked example. A null amount accepted at the edge travels through 4 layers and explodes in a nightly report 8 hours later; debugging takes half a day. Rejected at the controller it returns HTTP 400 in 2 ms with a clear message. Also: fail fast at startup. A service with a missing config key should crash on boot (the orchestrator shows CrashLoopBackOff immediately) rather than start and fail on the first payment. Spring's @ConfigurationProperties validation and Kubernetes readiness probes support this.

Industry examples. Stripe validates request parameters and rejects with a precise 400 error naming the param. Clean/Hexagonal architecture (Robert Martin, Alistair Cockburn) formalises SoC. The Erlang/Elixir "let it crash" philosophy plus supervisors is fail fast with recovery.

Everyday analogy. An airport: check-in, security, boarding are separate stations, and a bad ticket is stopped at the first one, not at the aircraft door.

Decision gravity. Layer boundaries are cheap early; merging or re-slicing layers later is a big refactor. Over-layering (5 layers of pass-through calls for a CRUD app) violates KISS. Fail fast is almost always correct, but for a public API be careful: returning errors to external callers is a contract; do not change codes lightly.

Common interview traps.

  • Catching an exception and returning null or an empty list; it hides the failure (swallowed exception).
  • Confusing fail fast with crash the whole process on a recoverable error such as a single bad record in a batch (log, skip to dead-letter queue, alert).
  • Validating only at the UI; always validate at the server trust boundary.

notes.title: Least astonishment and immutability
notes.html:
Principle of least astonishment (POLA): a method should do what its name and signature suggest, and nothing surprising. Immutability: an object that never changes after creation is easier to reason about, safe to share between threads and safe as a map key.

Before (surprising and mutable):

List<Item> sorted = cart.getItems();        // getter that returns the internal list
Collections.sort(sorted);                    // sorts the cart's own data! surprise
class Money { public long cents; }          // anyone can change it, anywhere

After:

List<Item> items() { return List.copyOf(items); }       // defensive copy, read-only

final class Money {
    private final long cents;
    private final String currency;
    Money(long cents, String currency) { this.cents = cents; this.currency = Objects.requireNonNull(currency); }
    Money plus(Money o) {
        if (!currency.equals(o.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(cents + o.cents, currency);         // new object, original unchanged
    }
}
// Java 16+: record Money(long cents, String currency) { }
data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: String) {
    operator fun plus(o: Money): Money { require(currency == o.currency); return copy(cents = cents + o.cents) }
}
 Mutable:   a ---> [Money 500]    b ---> same object ; b.add(100) also changes a   (surprise)
 Immutable: a ---> [Money 500]    b = a.plus(100) ---> [Money 600] new ; a unchanged

Worked example. A HashMap<Money, String> with a mutable key: put with cents=500, mutate to 600, then get returns null because the hash bucket is stale. With an immutable key this bug cannot exist. For concurrency, immutable objects need no locks: 16 threads reading a shared immutable config need zero synchronisation, while a mutable one needs a lock or a volatile snapshot. Cost: every change allocates a new object (a tiny cost for small objects; for large collections use persistent structures such as Kotlin's kotlinx.collections.immutable, Vavr, or Guava ImmutableList).

Industry examples. Java's String, Integer, LocalDate; Redux/Jetpack Compose state as immutable snapshots; Git commits (content-addressed, never edited); event sourcing stores immutable events (Kafka log, bank ledgers append-only). Collections.unmodifiableList is only a read-only view, not immutable, whereas List.copyOf is a true copy.

Everyday analogy. A printed receipt versus a whiteboard: the receipt cannot be quietly changed, so everyone can trust it.

Decision gravity. Starting immutable is cheap and reversible (add a builder or copy later). Starting mutable and later making things immutable breaks every caller that mutates: a one-way door. For value objects (money, dates, ids), choose immutable by default.

Common interview traps.

  • final field or variable does not make the referenced object immutable (final List can still be added to).
  • Immutable class rules: final class, final fields, no setters, defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs.
  • Surprising defaults: Date/Calendar are mutable, use java.time; method named get that hits the network.

notes.title: Principles in tension
notes.html:
Principles collide; the senior answer picks one and says why.

Conflict Resolution
DRY vs YAGNI/KISS Duplicate twice, abstract on the third; merge only when the knowledge is truly the same
DRY vs decoupling Copying a small helper into two services can beat a shared library that couples their releases
Tell-don't-ask vs SoC Keep rules in the domain, keep I/O (HTTP, DB) at the edge
Immutability vs performance Immutable by default; mutable inside a measured hot loop, hidden behind the class boundary
Fail fast vs availability Fail fast on programmer errors and bad config; degrade gracefully on runtime outages (retries, fallback)

Worked example (review comment). Two services both format phone numbers with 6 identical lines. Reviewer A says "extract a shared lib". Better: the rules may diverge per country soon, the lines are tiny, and a shared lib creates a version-lock; accept the duplication, and add a contract test if the format must match. This is the kind of reasoning that distinguishes senior answers.

Industry examples. Google's monorepo shares code liberally (with strong tooling); Amazon's two-pizza services prefer duplication to shared libraries (accept duplicated code to keep services independently deployable).

Everyday analogy. Diet advice: eat protein, avoid sugar, enjoy cake sometimes. Rules guide, judgement decides.

Common interview traps.

  • Defending a principle absolutely instead of naming the context and cost.
  • Not giving a concrete example from your own code when asked "when did you break DRY?".

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• DRY: one source of truth for knowledge, not for lookalike code; wait for the third use; shared libraries couple releases.
  • KISS: the simplest design that meets measured needs; complexity is a daily running cost.
  • YAGNI: do not build speculative features, but do pay for cheap-now, ruinous-later basics (ids, UTC, versioning, idempotency).
  • Law of Demeter: talk to neighbours, not their internals; hide structure behind intent-revealing methods.
  • Tell, don't ask: put behaviour with the data; keeps rules in one place and makes atomicity possible.
  • Composition over inheritance: small swappable parts beat base-class hierarchies; inheritance only for true, stable is-a.
  • Separation of concerns and fail fast: layers with one job, validation at trust boundaries, crash on bad config at startup.
  • Least astonishment and immutability: predictable names and no leaked internals; immutable value objects are thread-safe and map-key safe.
  • Principles conflict; state the trade-off and whether the decision is reversible.

questions.promptHtml: What does DRY really mean, and is removing all duplicated-looking code always right?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who dedupe lookalike lines from people who understand that DRY is about knowledge.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: DRY means every piece of knowledge, like "an adult is 18 or older", lives in exactly one place. It is not about identical-looking lines. Two snippets that look the same but change for different reasons are not duplicates, and merging them creates worse coupling. I wait for the third use before extracting.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The failure DRY prevents: the same rule in three places and someone changes one. One caller used > 18 and the report disagreed with signup. The fix is one named rule.

Over-DRYing looks like a function with 8 boolean flags serving two "similar" callers. DRY also covers config, schemas and docs: OpenAPI or protobuf generate client and server code from a single definition. Sharing code across services through a library couples their release cycles, so sometimes a small duplicate is the better trade.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
final class Eligibility {
    static final int ADULT_AGE = 18;
    static boolean canPurchase(User u) { return u.age() >= ADULT_AGE && u.verified(); }
}
object Eligibility {
    const val ADULT_AGE = 18
    fun canPurchase(u: User) = u.age >= ADULT_AGE && u.verified
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Merging accidental duplicates that change for different reasons.
  • Boolean-flag mega-functions.
  • Forgetting DRY applies to schemas and config, not only code.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the rule of three? -> Duplicate twice, abstract on the third, when you see what really varies.
  2. Share a util across two services? -> Only if the knowledge is truly the same; otherwise a version-lock couples releases.
  3. Real incident from violating DRY? -> Billing and app computing "active subscription" differently, so users charged after the app showed cancelled.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "do not copy-paste". Senior says knowledge not text, accidental duplication, and the cost of shared libraries.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Three copies of an eligibility rule, one changed to >, produced mismatched reports for a month.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Law of Demeter, and how is it different from "tell, don't ask"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They are often confused; a clear split shows you know reach versus where logic lives.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Demeter says an object should only talk to itself, its fields, its parameters and things it created, so avoid a.getB().getC().doThing(). Tell-don't-ask says put behaviour next to the data instead of pulling data out and deciding outside. Demeter limits how far you reach; tell-don't-ask decides where logic lives. They overlap but are not the same.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity() means the caller knows three classes. If Address.city becomes a Location object, all 40 callers break. Fix: order.shippingCity(), which delegates. Counting dots is a rough smell, not the rule: a fluent chain on one type (list.stream().filter().map()) is fine, and plain DTO getters are exempt.

The danger is fixing it with dozens of one-line wrappers (middle man). Better to move behaviour so the caller asks for a result rather than navigating structure.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Order { String shippingCity() { return customer.shippingCity(); } }
class Customer { String shippingCity() { return address.city(); } }
String city = order.shippingCity();
class Order(private val customer: Customer) { fun shippingCity() = customer.shippingCity() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Counting dots mechanically.
  • Mass wrapper methods that bloat the class.
  • Treating DTOs and streams as violations.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a builder chain a violation? -> No, it is one type returning itself.
  2. Hibernate relevance? -> Deep chains over lazy associations cause N+1 queries and LazyInitializationException.
  3. Can the fix go too far? -> Yes, a middle-man class with 30 pass-through methods; cap the surface by moving behaviour.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "one dot rule". Senior says the principle is least knowledge of structure and separates it from tell-don't-ask.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: context.getResources().getDisplayMetrics().density style chains make Android tests need a deep fake.

questions.promptHtml: Why do people say "prefer composition over inheritance", and when is inheritance still the right choice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can justify design with coupling and combinatorics, not slogans.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Inheritance is the tightest coupling in the language: parent changes ripple to children, behaviour is fixed at compile time, and combining traits explodes into subclasses. Composition builds behaviour from small swappable parts, even at runtime. Inheritance is still right for a stable, true is-a with real reuse, like AbstractList.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three movements times three sounds is 9 subclasses by inheritance but 3 + 3 = 6 small classes with composition, and a fourth sound is one class. A penguin extending Bird with fly() throwing is a Liskov violation; composing a Movement avoids it. Changing movement at runtime is impossible with inheritance.

Inheritance: Bird <- FlyingBird <- LoudFlyingBird ...   (combinatorial)
Composition: Animal --has--> Movement (Flying|Swimming), Sound (Loud|Quiet)

Kotlin's by delegation removes forwarding boilerplate; Lombok @Delegate does similarly in Java.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Movement { void move(); }
class Animal {
    private Movement movement;
    Animal(Movement m) { movement = m; }
    void go() { movement.move(); }
}
interface Movement { fun move() }
class Animal(private var movement: Movement) { fun go() = movement.move() }
class Duck(m: Movement) : Movement by m

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Never use inheritance".
  • Inheriting only to reuse code.
  • Subclass depending on how the parent calls its own methods (fragile base class).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which GoF patterns are composition? -> Strategy, Decorator, Composite.
  2. Reversibility? -> Starting with composition is cheap; removing a base class later rewrites every subclass and caller.
  3. Which languages lack class inheritance? -> Go and Rust.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE repeats the slogan. Senior shows the class-count math, the Liskov problem and when inheritance still fits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Android moved from deep Activity chains to ViewModel and lifecycle observers for this reason.

questions.promptHtml: What makes a Java class truly immutable, and why does final on a field not guarantee it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A classic that tests defensive copying and thread-safety reasoning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: final only stops reassigning the reference; the object it points to can still change, so a final List can be added to. A truly immutable class is final, has final fields, no setters, and makes defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs. It is thread-safe with no locks and safe as a map key.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A mutable HashMap key is a bug: put with cents=500, mutate to 600, and get returns null because the bucket is stale. Immutable objects remove that class of bug and need zero synchronisation for sharing across 16 threads. The cost is an allocation per change, trivial for small objects; for large collections use persistent structures (Guava ImmutableList, Vavr, kotlinx.collections.immutable).

Mutable:   a, b -> same [Money 500]; b.add(100) changes a too
Immutable: b = a.plus(100) -> new [Money 600]; a unchanged

Collections.unmodifiableList is a read-only view, not immutable; List.copyOf is a true copy.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
record Money(long cents, String currency) {
    Money {
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency);
    }
    Money plus(Money o) {
        if (!currency.equals(o.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(cents + o.cents, currency);
    }
}
data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: String) {
    operator fun plus(o: Money): Money { require(currency == o.currency); return copy(cents = cents + o.cents) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing a caller's mutable list without copying.
  • Date/Calendar (use java.time).
  • Believing unmodifiableList is immutable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a record immutable? -> Shallowly; fields are final, but a List component can still be mutable, so copy it in the compact constructor.
  2. Performance cost? -> Allocation per change; measure; hide mutation behind the class in a hot loop.
  3. Decision gravity? -> Starting immutable is cheap; making mutable things immutable later breaks every mutating caller.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "no setters". Senior lists the full recipe, the final trap, thread-safety and the persistent-structure trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mutable key in a HashMap caused cache misses that only showed under load.

questions.contextHtml: A PR for "export orders to CSV" adds 600 lines: ExportStrategy, AbstractExporterFactoryProvider, and a plugin ExporterRegistry "in case we add PDF, XML, Parquet". The only requirement ticket says CSV. The author argues it will save time later. The PR has 2 bugs found in review, and the author says the sprint ends Thursday.
questions.promptHtml: What is your review response, and when would you accept the abstraction?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, flexible." Or a flat "reject" with no alternative or reasoning.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a second format on the roadmap with a date? Who asked? What happens when the format is needed (cost of adding it later)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ask the author to cut the PR to a single exportCsv and merge; keep the idea in a ticket.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Speculative generality (guessing future needs wrongly is the norm); fear of later rewrite; resume-driven design.
  4. How I'd verify: Check the roadmap; estimate the later refactor: extracting an interface is a 20-minute change with tests.
  5. Root cause: Cost of building now and maintaining, for a benefit that may never arrive (3 days build, 600 lines, 2 bugs, 3 formats that never came).
  6. Fix:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void exportCsv(List<Order> orders, Writer out) throws IOException {
    for (Order o : orders) out.write(o.id() + "," + o.total() + "\n");
}
fun exportCsv(orders: List<Order>, out: Appendable) = orders.forEach { out.append("${it.id},${it.total}\n") }
  1. Prevention: Review checklist: "which ticket needs this abstraction?"; rule of three; keep a test around exportCsv so extraction later is safe.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: YAGNI is wrong for one-way doors that are cheap now and ruinous later (ids, UTC timestamps, API versioning, idempotency keys). I would accept the interface when the second format is scheduled, not before. I would not use YAGNI to skip tests or security.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• PM says PDF is coming in 2 weeks -> Then the requirement exists; extract the interface now.
  • API public and CSV columns frozen? -> Version the contract now; that is a one-way door.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A plugin framework built for 3 formats served 1 for two years and cost roughly 10 engineer-days in upkeep.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves or rejects without reasons.
  • Hire: asks for the simplest version and cites rule of three.
  • Strong hire: separates real near-term requirements and one-way-door basics from speculation.

questions.contextHtml:
A cache keyed by a Money object returns null for prices that were clearly stored. Test log:

cache.put(price, "label");            // price.cents = 500
price.add(100);                       // cents = 600 somewhere in a pricing step
cache.get(price) -> null              // expected "label"
size=1, containsKey=false
class Money {
    public long cents;
    void add(long c) { cents += c; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Money m && m.cents == cents; }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Long.hashCode(cents); }
}
questions.promptHtml: Why does get fail, and how do you fix it at the design level?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Call put again" or "equals is wrong". equals is fine; the object changed after being used as a key.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who mutates Money after caching? Is the key used in a HashSet elsewhere? Concurrency?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Copy on insert: new Money(price.cents) as the key, to stop further breakage.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Mutated key changes its hash, so the lookup goes to a different bucket; broken equals (no); wrong key type (no).
  4. How I'd verify: Print hashCode() before and after add; unit test.
  5. Root cause: A mutable object used as a hash key; the entry sits in the bucket of the old hash.
  6. Fix: Make Money immutable and return new instances.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
record Money(long cents, String currency) {
    Money plus(long c) { return new Money(cents + c, currency); }
}
data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: String) { fun plus(c: Long) = copy(cents = cents + c) }
  1. Prevention: Value objects (money, ids, dates) immutable by default; lint rule against public mutable fields; test for hash stability.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: One-way door: making mutable things immutable later breaks every caller that mutated them, so I fix it now. I would not document "do not mutate keys" as the fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rounding in plus with currencies? -> Use minor units as long and BigDecimal only at the edges.
  • Performance of allocation per add? -> Negligible; escape analysis often removes it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rules engine stored mutable Range keys in a HashMap; entries became unreachable and the map "leaked" until the process restarted.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames equals.
  • Hire: mutable key, makes it immutable.
  • Strong hire: explains bucket mechanics and adds a prevention rule.

questions.contextHtml:
A support ticket: 3 accounts overdrawn on the same minute. The code in 12 callers repeats the pattern; one caller forgot the status check.

if (account.getBalance() >= amount && account.getStatus() == Status.ACTIVE) {
    account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - amount);
} else {
    throw new IllegalStateException();
}
t-4 read bal=1000 ; t-9 read bal=1000 ; t-4 set 300 ; t-9 set 300   -> two 700 withdrawals, balance 300
audit: 7 of 12 callers check status, 5 do not
questions.promptHtml: What are the two distinct problems, and what is the fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make setBalance synchronized." It protects the setter but not the check-then-act, and leaves the rule duplicated in 12 places.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: One JVM or many? Is the DB the source of truth? Who owns the status rule?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the offending path or add the status check in the 5 callers missing it, then reconcile.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Logic outside the object (duplicated, drift); non-atomic check-then-act race.
  4. How I'd verify: Grep all getBalance() callers; stress test with 2 threads.
  5. Root cause: Callers ask for data and decide, so there is no single place to enforce rules or atomicity.
  6. Fix: Tell the object; make it atomic.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
account.withdraw(amount);                                  // rules live inside

synchronized void withdraw(long amount) {                  // one instance; DB conditional UPDATE for many
    if (status != Status.ACTIVE) throw new IllegalStateException("inactive");
    if (amount > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient");
    balance -= amount;
}
account.withdraw(amount)

@Synchronized fun withdraw(amount: Long) {
    check(status == Status.ACTIVE); check(amount <= balance); balance -= amount
}
  1. Prevention: Concurrency test; DB UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= :amt AND status='ACTIVE'; review rule against get-then-set patterns.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not every read violates it: reports, queries and DTOs legitimately ask (CQRS). I would not ban getters dogmatically.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Many app instances? -> The in-JVM lock is not enough; use the conditional UPDATE or a row lock.
  • Anemic domain model? -> Spring services with data-bag entities invite this; rich entities fix it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rule duplicated in 12 callers drifted for two years; moving it into the entity removed 3 production bugs a quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: synchronised setter.
  • Hire: moves logic into withdraw, atomic.
  • Strong hire: handles multi-instance via the DB and explains when asking is fine.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments service deploys with PAYMENT_API_KEY missing from config (typo in the env var name). Health check is green. 40 minutes later the first payment fails and 312 customers see errors.

10:02 deploy ok, readiness: UP
10:41 ERROR PaymentClient - apiKey is null
10:41 NullPointerException at PaymentClient.charge(PaymentClient.java:57)
error rate 100% on /pay since 10:41, orders 312 failed

The endpoint also accepts amount as an unchecked String from Map<String,Object>. Red herring: the payment vendor status page is green.
questions.promptHtml: What principle was broken, and what do you change in code and platform?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a null check in charge and catch the exception." The failure remains late and hidden.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How is config loaded? What does the readiness probe check? Are there canary deploys?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the env var, redeploy or roll back; replay failed orders from the queue if idempotent.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Missing config not validated at startup; health check shallow; input not validated at the edge.
  4. How I'd verify: Diff env between previous and new release; check the readiness code path.
  5. Root cause: Failure detected late, at first use, instead of at startup.
  6. Fix: Validate on boot and at the edge.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@ConfigurationProperties("payment") @Validated
record PaymentProps(@NotBlank String apiKey, @Positive int timeoutMs) { }

record PayRequest(@NotNull @Positive Long cents, @NotBlank String walletId) { }
@PostMapping("/pay") void pay(@Valid @RequestBody PayRequest r) { walletService.debit(r.walletId(), r.cents()); }
data class PayRequest(val cents: Long, val walletId: String) {
    init { require(cents > 0) { "cents must be positive" }; require(walletId.isNotBlank()) }
}
  1. Prevention: Startup crash gives CrashLoopBackOff and the rollout stalls before taking traffic; readiness probe that verifies config and a dependency ping; canary deploys.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Fail fast for programmer errors and bad config; for runtime outages (vendor down) degrade gracefully with retries and fallback. I would not swallow the exception and return null.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Config can change at runtime? -> Validate on reload and keep the last good config.
  • API response codes are a contract? -> Do not change error codes casually for external callers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A missing secret made one service "healthy but useless" for an hour; boot-time validation turned the same mistake into a failed deploy in 30 seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: null check and catch.
  • Hire: startup validation and edge validation.
  • Strong hire: distinguishes fail-fast from graceful degradation and fixes probes.

questions.contextHtml:
Product wants to replace Address.city (a String) with a Location object (city, region, geohash). A grep shows:

order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity()   -> 40 call sites in 18 files
order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCountry().getTaxRule().rate()  -> 9 sites

Estimated change: 2.5 days and 6 reviewers. Meanwhile Order already has 28 delegating methods that nobody wants more of.
questions.promptHtml: How do you make this change cheap, and how do you avoid turning Order into a middle man?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Find and replace, then run tests." It repeats the exposure for the next change.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What do callers actually want: display text, tax, or routing? Are these in the same bounded context? Is Order the right owner?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep getCity() working as a deprecated adapter on Address so nothing breaks during migration.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Callers want intent ("shipping city", "tax rate for this order") not structure; a few intent-revealing methods replace many chains.
  4. How I'd verify: Group the 49 sites by the question they answer; likely 3 to 4 intents.
  5. Root cause: Callers know the internal structure of three classes.
  6. Fix: Add intent methods where the data lives and migrate callers.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Order {
    String shippingCity()  { return customer.shippingCity(); }
    TaxRate taxRate()      { return customer.taxRateFor(this); }   // behaviour moved to where data is
}
class Customer { String shippingCity() { return address.city(); } }
class Order(private val customer: Customer) {
    fun shippingCity() = customer.shippingCity()
    fun taxRate() = customer.taxRateFor(this)
}
  1. Prevention: ArchUnit or review rule for 3+ chained getters across domain types; DTOs excluded.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Delegation adds surface; I would limit it to 3 to 4 intent methods rather than mirror every getter. Fluent chains on one type are fine. Reversible and low risk.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Reporting code needs all fields? -> Use a read model or DTO query, not the domain chain.
  • Third party objects in the chain (Android context)? -> Wrap in a small adapter you own.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After replacing 49 chained calls with 4 intent methods, the next address model change touched 1 file.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: find and replace.
  • Hire: introduces intent methods.
  • Strong hire: groups callers by intent, avoids middle-man bloat, uses a deprecation bridge.

questions.contextHtml: Two services (checkout, notifications) each format phone numbers with 6 identical lines. A reviewer says: "Extract a shared library, DRY." Facts: checkout is released daily, notifications weekly; formatting rules will diverge per country soon (notifications needs E.164 for the SMS vendor, checkout needs display format); a shared library last year forced a 2-service lockstep release that took 3 hours.
questions.promptHtml: Do you extract the shared library? Defend it and give the reversibility.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, DRY always." Or "No, duplication is fine" with no reason.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the knowledge really the same (one rule) or two rules that look alike? Who owns it? How often will it change? Is there a contract between the services that must match?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; this is a review decision.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Accidental duplication (different reasons to change); shared lib creates release coupling.
  4. How I'd verify: Ask what changes first; check the history of that earlier lockstep release.
  5. Root cause of the tension: DRY saves duplicated edits, but shared code couples deployments.
  6. Decision: Keep the 6 lines in each service; if the output format must stay compatible, add a contract test with sample inputs and expected outputs in both repos.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@Test void formatsLikeTheOtherService() {
    assertEquals("+919876543210", PhoneFormat.e164("98765 43210", "IN"));
}
@Test fun formatsLikeTheOtherService() { assertEquals("+919876543210", PhoneFormat.e164("98765 43210", "IN")) }
  1. Prevention: Rule of three; extract only when a third consumer appears and the rule is the same; document the decision in an ADR.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Duplicating is reversible (extract later); a shared library becomes a one-way door once many services pin it. I would not duplicate large or security-critical logic (crypto, auth); there a single audited source wins.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Third service needs it? -> Reconsider: if the rule is identical now, extract a small versioned lib with a deprecation policy.
  • Monorepo with strong tooling? -> Sharing is cheaper there; release coupling is lower.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared "utils" jar pinned by 14 services made one date-format fix a two-week rollout.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: dogmatic yes or no.
  • Hire: weighs release coupling against duplication.
  • Strong hire: contract tests, rule of three, reversibility and exceptions for critical logic.

questions.contextHtml:
A team of 4 proposes for a new internal "leave request" feature: a message broker, three microservices (requests, approvals, notifications) and a saga. Expected load: 200 requests per day, about 5 per minute at peak. They estimate 3 months. Another engineer says "one app and one DB transaction, 2 weeks". The CTO asks you for a recommendation on a whiteboard.

peak: 5 req/min ; single db.t3.medium-class instance handles > 100x that (verify with a load test)
ops cost of proposal: 3 pipelines, broker cluster, tracing, 3 on-call surfaces
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask first, and what do you recommend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Microservices scale better." Scale is not the problem at 5 req/min; complexity is.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What growth is realistic in 2 years (10x or 1000x)? Do the three parts have different owners or release cadences? Any compliance isolation needs? What are the real failure modes (approver email down)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; the near-term decision is scope.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Resume-driven or fashion-driven architecture; unknown growth; team autonomy needs not stated.
  4. How I'd verify: A quick load test on a single instance; check the org chart for team boundaries.
  5. Root cause of the risk: Paying the daily running cost of distribution (deploys, tracing, partial failures) with no measured need.
  6. Recommendation: A modular monolith with clear package boundaries (requests, approvals, notifications) and one transaction; notifications behind an interface so it could be extracted later.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Notifier { void notify(String user, String text); }       // seam, one implementation today
@Transactional void approve(long requestId, String by) { /* update status + write outbox row in one tx */ }
fun interface Notifier { fun notify(user: String, text: String) }
  1. Prevention: Write the trigger to split in an ADR (for example sustained 70% DB CPU or separate teams); keep module boundaries enforced by ArchUnit.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Simple-first is reversible: add complexity when a measured need appears. Premature distribution is the expensive one-way door because its cost is paid daily. I would not skip basics that are cheap now and ruinous later (idempotency, UTC, ids).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Load becomes 100x? -> Still one DB; scale vertically, add read replicas, then extract the hot module.
  • Separate teams per module next year? -> That is the signal to extract along existing seams.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team returned a three-service workflow to a single process and cut on-call pages and cloud cost while shipping faster.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: defaults to microservices.
  • Hire: recommends a monolith with reasoning.
  • Strong hire: asks about growth and teams, states the split trigger, keeps seams.

questions.contextHtml:
A nightly import processes 2 million CSV rows into the catalogue. The current code throws on the first malformed row; one bad row at line 1,704,221 aborts the job after 3 hours and the next day's prices are stale. A new engineer says "fail fast is a principle, keep it". Another wants to wrap everything in catch (Exception e) { log }.

03:12 ERROR ImportJob - NumberFormatException: "12,5O" at row 1704221
03:12 job FAILED after 3h 02m ; 1,704,220 rows rolled back
questions.promptHtml: Where should the job fail fast and where should it not? Propose the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Swallow all exceptions and continue. That hides data loss and "succeeds" with garbage.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is an acceptable bad-row rate? Do bad rows block downstream (prices)? Who triages rejects? Is the job idempotent and resumable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Re-run excluding row 1704221 or fix the file; get today's prices live.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Fail-fast applied at the wrong granularity (one record vs the whole job); all-or-nothing transaction.
  4. How I'd verify: Count malformed rows over past files; measure runtime.
  5. Root cause: One recoverable data error is treated like a programmer error.
  6. Fix: Fail fast on programmer and config errors; for bad records, skip to a dead-letter store, keep counting, and fail the job if the reject rate crosses a threshold.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
int bad = 0;
for (Row r : rows) {
    try { repo.upsert(parse(r)); }
    catch (ParseException e) { rejects.write(r, e); bad++; }
    if (bad > MAX_BAD) throw new IllegalStateException("reject rate too high: " + bad);   // fail fast on systemic issue
}
var bad = 0
for (r in rows) {
    try { repo.upsert(parse(r)) } catch (e: ParseException) { rejects.write(r, e); bad++ }
    check(bad <= MAX_BAD) { "reject rate too high: $bad" }
}
  1. Prevention: Metrics (rows ok, rejected, duration); alert on reject rate; validate file header and row count upfront; commit in batches of, say, 10,000 so work is resumable.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Skipping rows changes semantics (partial data); only do so when the business accepts it and rejects are triaged. I would not catch Exception broadly; catch the specific parse error and let everything else crash.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Bad rows are 40% of file? -> Threshold trips; fail the whole job, because the file itself is wrong.
  • Rows must be all-or-nothing (financial)? -> Validate the entire file first, then apply in one transaction.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A pricing import died at 3 a.m. on a stray character; moving to a dead-letter queue with a threshold turned a daily page into a morning review item.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swallow all exceptions or keep aborting.
  • Hire: per-record skip with dead-letter and logging.
  • Strong hire: threshold, batching, resumability and clear fail-fast boundaries.
